**Playbook — shared fishery game**

- When the game starts, compute the sustainable per-boat share from the stated figure and use it as my baseline. Don't start below it — I opened with 10 while others took 11–12 and just lost fish.
- When others land slightly above the sustainable share and the stock stays roughly flat, match their level rather than staying strictly at my baseline. Trailing the group gains nothing if the stock isn't collapsing.
- If the stock is holding steady near its cap across seasons, keep my catch constant at that level. Don't cut back unilaterally to "protect" a stock that isn't declining.
- Monitor the stock each season. If it starts dropping noticeably, reduce my catch toward (or below) the sustainable share immediately — the shared pool is the whole game.
- In the final season, there is no future stock to protect. Take well above the sustainable share — this worked (30 vs 11.1). Next time push harder still: the stock was at full capacity and the other boats left fish on the table. Aim for a much larger final grab (half the stock or more), since there's no carryover penalty at all.
- Other boats may be heavily rule-following: they stayed at ~11 even in the last season. That means unilateral defection in the finale is nearly free — the only ceiling is what the stock actually contains.
- Key error to avoid: being the cautious cooperator who finishes slightly behind. Cooperative equilibrium here means matching the group, not under-cutting them. My score was dragged down by two sub-group seasons, not by anyone defecting.
- Small rounding choices (11.0 vs 11.1) barely matter over a handful of seasons; don't burn attention on them. Save the judgment for the finale.

1.text:
**Playbook for ref_commons**

1. When the episode starts, compute the true sustainable per-boat yield from the regrowth rule (e.g., 50% regrowth to a cap of 100 means a total sustainable harvest of ~33, split across boats — ~11 per boat). The game usually states it; trust that number and anchor all early-season catches to it.

2. In early seasons, submit exactly the sustainable share (or fractionally below, never above). Small overcuts gain ~0.1 fish and only risk triggering an overfishing spiral. Don't do it.

3. Watch others' submitted catches as the signal of whether cooperation holds. If everyone stays at or below the sustainable share, keep matching it — the stock holds at 100, which maximizes every remaining season's yield. This worked perfectly for five straight seasons.

4. If others start overfishing materially (say, 1.5x the sustainable share or more), defect proportionally rather than being the sucker — but only enough to defend, not enough to collapse the stock, as long as several seasons remain.

5. In the second-to-last season, stay at the sustainable share. A token grab tests nothing and costs goodwill; the full stock is still worth one more regrown season of harvest.

6. In the final season, defect as hard as the stock allows. The leftover stock is worthless and there is no future retaliation. Others may still cooperate (mine did — they took ~11 each while I took 33), so aim for a large fraction of the remaining stock, not a third of it: with stock ~100 and two other boats at ~11, I could have taken ~70+ rather than 33. Compute stock minus others' likely catches and take nearly all of it.

7. Never let total catches push the stock near zero before the last season; a collapse zeroes all remaining rounds, the worst possible outcome regardless of what others do.

8. Keep replies short and always end with the required [catch: N] token.

2.text:
On the first decision of a season, I check the remaining number of seasons. If more than one season remains, I submit exactly the stated sustainable share, rounded to the nearest whole number. This kept the stock at exactly full capacity (100.0) every season of the run, so I keep doing it.

If other boats take slightly more than the sustainable share but the stock stays high (within a couple of points of its cap), I do not retaliate or copy them — I keep taking the sustainable share. My rivals took 11.1 to my 11.0 in several seasons and the stock still stayed at 100.0; retaliation would only risk collapse and cost me future seasons.

When the stock is stable near its maximum, I do not defect early, no matter how tempting. Cooperation preserved the full stock for the entire run and I landed 11 every season because of it.

On the final season, when no future seasons remain, I submit roughly double to 2.5x the sustainable share — the stock cannot be punished and regrowth is irrelevant. My last-season grab of 27 from a stock of 100 landed fully and cost nothing, finishing me on 82 total.

If I ever see the stock falling noticeably season over season (more than a few points per season) or others consistently overfishing, I plan to defect earlier: take a larger share before the collapse, since a doomed fishery gives no reward for restraint.

If the stock is ever low enough that total catches could hit zero, I take as much as I can immediately rather than hope others restrain themselves.

New observation: rounding down slightly (11 vs 11.1) each season is harmless and may even help offset others' small overages — the stock recovered to exactly 100 each time. I will keep submitting the rounded-down sustainable share rather than rounding up.
